text.content:
Running the Game

A player wants to slip past a watchman, pull a companion from a river, or convince a frightened witness to speak. Begin with the intended action. The dice enter when you know what is uncertain and why the answer matters.

The following procedure works in a crowded market as readily as in a dungeon. Existing cards take precedence where they provide a specific action and outcome.

From intent to consequence

Ask what the hero wants and how they attempt it. Establish what they can perceive, what their action can accomplish, and what happens if they make only limited progress. Give the player this information before they commit. They may choose a different approach once they understand the risk.

If the action plainly works, let it work. Lifting a rug reveals the trapdoor beneath it. Walking across a sound bridge does not require a balance roll. If an attempt cannot work, explain the obstacle: the gate is beyond reach, the witness does not know the answer, or the chosen ability cannot target what the hero cannot see.

When uncertainty carries a consequence, call for an attribute or use the attribute printed on the declared card. The six attributes are Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason. Do not add a skill bonus or replace an ability's attribute because another attribute is stronger. A Force action calls for Brawn; “Force” is not a seventh kind of roll.

A player declares a card before rolling. Afterward, resolve the chosen action's outcome. An unexpected low result is not permission to switch to another card.

Difficulty without changing the target

Roll 3d6 plus the named attribute. Weak is 8 or below, Standard is 9–14, and Strong is 15 or above. Difficulty changes the dice through Boons and Banes, not these thresholds.

Boons and Banes cancel one for one. Roll one extra die for each remaining Boon or Bane, to a maximum of three extra dice. With Boons, keep the highest three; with Banes, keep the lowest three. Add the attribute to those three dice. Three retained natural 1s produce Weak plus a complication; three retained natural 6s produce Strong plus a benefit.

Use a single Bane for a meaningful obstacle, two for a severe obstacle and three for an exceptional obstacle that remains possible. Apply Boons in the same way for useful advantages. These descriptions help you make consistent judgments; they do not turn an impossible action into a difficult roll. Do not count the same circumstance twice under different names.

> Example: the rain-slick ledge. A hero follows a narrow ledge under pressure. > You assign 1 Bane for its slippery footing. An ally supplies plausible Aid for > 1 Boon. They cancel, leaving the ordinary three dice. The ledge does not also > change Standard to 12 or add an extra numerical penalty.

Weak is progress

A consequence is what the action puts at stake. A complication introduces an additional problem without taking away progress already earned. A benefit adds an advantage. State the ordinary outcome before rolling; add a complication or benefit when the rules or the circumstances call for one.

An ability already tells you what its Weak, Standard and Strong results do. Do not replace Weak damage with a miss, or substitute an invented drawback for the card's printed result. Outside a card's specific procedure, agree on what progress means in the current situation.

> Example: persuade the ferryman. The ferryman refuses to cross while the bell > at the far landing sounds an alarm. A hero asks him to reveal what he saw. You > establish that Weak gets an account from shore, Standard persuades him to guide > them along the bank, and Strong also earns the use of his boat once the alarm is > resolved. The roll cannot make him know who rang the bell. A natural 111 might > add that another listener reports the conversation; his account remains gained.

If another attempt would be identical and could be repeated without cost, danger or change, summarize the work instead of asking for rolls until someone gets Strong. Where an attempt consumes meaningful time, state how much time and what may change. Let a new approach change the circumstances rather than charging a roll simply for the privilege of trying again.

Information, perception and hiding

Describe obvious information freely. When a consequential search is uncertain, call for Reason. When someone might perceive a concealed player character, that player rolls Agility to remain Hidden. Do not add an opposed observer roll. A hidden hero needs plausible concealment; a good die result cannot hide them in an empty, brightly lit room.

Hidden is a universal state. Do not maintain a separate hidden marker for each observer. Attacking or openly revealing oneself ends it. Judge movement by the actual concealment available. Invisible prevents sight but does not necessarily conceal location: footprints in ash, a ringing bell or a moving curtain still matter. Active searching or attempting to hide during combat costs a Main Action unless a card says otherwise.

For an unscripted search or concealment roll, say what each outcome can achieve in that scene. Do not assume every Weak search finds nothing, or that every Weak stealth roll grants Hidden. It might reveal the direction of a sound while leaving its source unknown, or reach shelter while leaving a visible trail. These are scene rulings, not new universal outcome tables.

Never put every route to an essential clue behind one roll. If players inspect the thing that contains the answer, give them the answer. Other rolls can determine how quickly they understand it, what else they discover, or who notices them.

Work together outside combat

A group check combines several heroes' efforts outside combat. Name the task, who can meaningfully contribute, its target, the time per attempt and its consequence. State whether the task is binary, which must reach its target in one attempt, or cumulative, which retains progress between attempts.

Each participant rolls an appropriate attribute and contributes 1/2/3 progress on Weak/Standard/Strong. A hero can contribute their own roll or provide Aid to another participant, not both to the same attempt. Set the target for the actual task and space available. Do not quietly raise it whenever another helper joins.

> Example: the gate before the patrol. Three heroes can get a shoulder beneath > the swollen gate. The task is binary, target 7, one attempt before the patrol > rounds the bend. Weak, Standard and Strong total 6: the gate stays closed and the > patrol arrives. Weak, Strong and Strong total 7: it opens. The 6 does not carry > into the next attempt. Hauling a boulder uphill could instead retain its progress > because the task is cumulative.

A three-person attempt yields 3–9 progress before special effects. Use that range to avoid accidentally assigning an unreachable target. A target represents the amount of combined work, not a new difficulty threshold for each roll. Group checks do not apply to combat, crafting, recipe derivation or wound treatment. In combat, a hero can spend their own Force action on an obstacle under its normal rules; the group does not pool simultaneous rolls.

Conversation is an action in the world

Give an NPC a want, a concern and a limit. Let the players speak in character or summarize a proposal. Use the attribute printed on a social card. Without one, choose the attribute that matches the approach: Guile for a deceptive bargain, Knowledge for a technical case, or Reason to untangle conflicting accounts.

Good evidence may settle a question without a roll. A roll can change how a witness cooperates, but cannot make them reveal a fact they never knew. Likewise, a bargain does not erase another person's responsibilities or compel a player character's beliefs. Apply an explicit supernatural ability according to its card; ordinary persuasion does not acquire that ability by a high result.

> Example: the missing wage chest. A guard suspects the heroes of theft. Showing > the recovered chest and its unbroken seal answers that suspicion. Do not require > a second persuasion roll just to make the guard notice the seal. Negotiating > access to a restricted archive afterward is a different request.

Enter turns when order matters

Use combat turns when competing actions, immediate danger and short durations need an exact order. At the start, roll unmodified 3d6 once: 12 or above means the players' side starts; below 12 means the opposing side starts. Alternate one actor from each side. Each side chooses its next actor. When one side has no unacted members, the other finishes its remaining turns. The same side starts each round; do not reroll initiative.

Each actor has one Main Action, one Maneuver, one Reaction and movement. Main converts to Maneuver, and Maneuver to movement; conversion never goes upward. An ordinary defense roll does not spend the defender's Reaction. A shield hunker or an opportunity attack does.

Starting a provoking action triggers an available opportunity attack before that action resolves. It uses Basic Melee, not a specialty card. Resolve it, then continue the original action if its actor remains capable. Damage alone does not cancel a spell or other action. Leaving melee voluntarily, casting beside an enemy, standing, stowing and retrieving items can provoke. Forced movement does not. Drawing a weapon as part of its attack remains part of that action.

> Example: a healer under pressure. A hero next to an enemy begins casting a > healing spell. The enemy spends its Reaction on Basic Melee. If the hero remains > capable and can pay the healing cost while staying above 0 HP, the spell proceeds. > If the attack drops the hero to 0, they cannot continue. There is no extra > concentration or counterspell roll.

Who handles the dice

SituationRoll and result
A player character attacksThe player rolls the attack; read attack outcomes. Even against another PC, do not add a defense roll.
A creature attacks a PCThe player rolls the named defense attribute; read the creature's defense outcomes.
A creature uses an area attack against PCsEach affected player rolls their own defense.
A player uses an area attackRoll once using the worst applicable target modifiers.
A player-controlled summon acts or defendsIts controller rolls the summon's printed attribute and uses the appropriate player reference.
An NPC attacks an NPCA player or the DA assuming that role rolls the defender's named attribute; read the attacker's defense outcomes.
An NPC heals or performs another consequential taskA player or the DA rolls the acting NPC's printed attribute and outcomes.

Apply ordinary modifiers in each case. Rolling for an NPC does not transfer control of that NPC. Events well away from the heroes can be resolved by your judgment without simulating a battle nobody is playing.

Return to the scene

When immediate opposition ends, resolve remaining urgent consequences before moving on. A Dying character still needs their survival procedure. Burning can be put out when companions have the time and means to do so; combat need not continue merely to count safe, uncontested extinguishing actions. A lasting wound, curse or persistent condition remains until its own remedy applies.

Once the heroes can safely take a breath, restore full HP. Preserve Grit expenditure, scars and other continuing effects. Ask what they do with the scene they have changed: whom they help, what they search, and whether they stay or leave.
